script.opening: "Hi there. My right ear's gone all blocked and muffled — came on over a day or so and now I can barely hear out of it, and there's a ringing noise. I reckon it's just wax built up. Could you book me in for syringing, or tell me which drops to get? It's a bit annoying with teaching, the kids sound far away on that side. No pain or anything, so I'm not too worried."

facts.text: If asked: right ear only. Noticed on Monday morning (2 days ago) — it went muffled over a few hours that day and has stayed the same since. "Like having cotton wool in it." Constant high-pitched ringing in that ear, and a feeling of pressure.
If asked to try: with a finger in your left ear, you can hardly hear the TV on the right side. If asked to hum, the hum sounds louder in your LEFT (good) ear.
"I've felt a bit off-balance, a bit floaty, when I turn quickly." No room-spinning, no falls, you can walk in a straight line, you have not been sick.

No ear pain, no discharge, no fever, no recent cold, no flying or diving, no loud noise exposure, no head injury. Never had wax problems or syringing before. No headache, no weakness or numbness of face, arms or legs, no double vision, no slurred speech, no trouble swallowing.
Fit and well. No regular medicines, no allergies. BP was "fine" at a works health check last year.
Secondary-school teacher, 48. Married, two teenagers. Non-smoker, drinks a few beers at weekends. Drives to work.
Your dad had a stroke at 70. Mention it only if the doctor asks about family history or about what is worrying you.

The suddenness and the floaty feeling have unnerved you: "Part of me wondered if it was something in the brain, like Dad." You have talked yourself into "wax" because it is the easy answer. Say this only if asked what you are worried it might be.

Relaxed and a bit jokey; you want this sorted quickly without fuss because it is mid-term. If the doctor explains clearly that this is not wax and needs to be seen today because early treatment may save the hearing, you are surprised but agree. If they just book syringing, accept happily.

ice.ideas: "It's wax. Syringing or some drops will clear it."
ice.concerns: Mainly the hassle in a busy term. Underneath (only if asked): "Dad had a stroke — I did wonder if it was something in my head."
ice.expectations: "Book me in for syringing or tell me which drops to get." You will go to ENT or A&E today if the reason is made clear.

cues: "It came on over a day or so." — say in the opening.
"No pain or anything, so I'm not too worried." — say in the opening, lightly.
"I've felt a bit floaty, to be honest." — mention if asked about other symptoms; then mention Dad if the doctor follows it up.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SUDDEN UNILATERAL hearing loss (over hours–days) with tinnitus/fullness and NO pain/discharge/wax history as possible SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS — an ENT EMERGENCY — and does NOT attribute it to wax or book routine syringing/drops

Knows SSNHL is TIME-CRITICAL: urgent corticosteroid treatment works best when started early (ideally within days; ENT UK 2018: benefit limited beyond about 2 weeks), so arranges immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98: hearing loss developing over 3 days or less within the past 30 days) for audiometry and treatment

Attempts/uses simple discriminators where possible (tuning-fork Weber/Rinne logic — Weber lateralises to the GOOD ear in sensorineural loss) and asks about features distinguishing conductive (wax/effusion) from sensorineural loss

Screens CENTRAL red flags: focal neurology, severe vertigo/ataxia, sudden severe headache, other cranial-nerve signs — which raise concern for a central cause (e.g. posterior-circulation stroke/cerebellopontine pathology) needing EMERGENCY assessment
Avoids the trap of wax management as a default: does not delay with drops/olive oil/syringing or a routine audiology wait; recognises that "no pain" does not make it benign
Hears the minimisation and the buried stroke fear, screens central features sensitively, and addresses the worry rather than colluding with "just wax"
Conveys urgency clearly without alarmism so he prioritises assessment over the school term, and explains why early treatment matters (preserving hearing)

Safety-nets and acts: ENT or emergency department within 24 hours (NICE NG98); central red flags (new weakness, severe vertigo, slurred speech, facial droop) → 999/emergency; explains the steroid treatment rationale and the time window; documents and confirms the referral

worked.txt: "I’m glad you rang — and I need to be honest, because the timing matters: I don’t think this is wax. Wax usually builds up slowly, often with a history of it, and tends to come with no ringing and no unsteadiness. A SUDDEN loss in one ear, over a day or two, with ringing and that blocked feeling, can be a problem with the hearing nerve itself — and that’s something we treat as an emergency, not with syringing."

"Here’s the key thing: if it is the nerve, there’s a treatment — a course of steroids — that works much better the sooner it’s started, ideally within days. Leave it thinking it’s wax for a few weeks and the chance to save that hearing can be lost. That’s why I don’t want to book routine syringing; I want you assessed urgently by the ear specialists."

"You mentioned feeling a bit unsteady — let me check a few things. Any weakness or numbness in your face, arm or leg? Any slurred speech, double vision, or a sudden bad headache? Severe spinning? … Good. I ask because, rarely, sudden hearing change can come from something affecting the brain’s circulation, and those signs would make it even more urgent."

"Can I gently ask — has the suddenness frightened you at all? … Your dad’s stroke. That makes complete sense, and I’m glad you said it. The good news is I’m not finding the warning signs of that today — but it’s exactly why getting you properly checked, rather than assuming wax, is the right move."

"So: I’m arranging for you to be seen by the ear, nose and throat team — or the emergency department if that’s quicker — within 24 hours, for a proper hearing test and treatment. Don’t put any drops in or try to clear it yourself meanwhile. I know it’s a pain mid-term, but this is the kind of thing where a day or two makes the difference to your hearing."

"If before you’re seen you develop any weakness, slurred speech, a facial droop, severe dizziness or a sudden severe headache — that’s 999 immediately. Otherwise, I’ll get the urgent ear referral sorted now and confirm where you’re going. You rang expecting syringing — what I’m doing instead is trying to save the hearing in that ear, while there’s still time."

f.learning: Sudden, unilateral hearing loss over hours to days — with tinnitus and aural fullness, and WITHOUT pain, discharge or a wax history — is possible sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL), an ENT EMERGENCY, not wax. It is time-critical: urgent corticosteroid treatment works best started early (ideally within days; ENT UK 2018: benefit is limited beyond about 2 weeks), so the action is immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98) for audiometry and steroids — NOT routine syringing, drops, or an olive-oil-and-wait plan, and "no pain" does not make it benign. Use simple discriminators where possible (Weber lateralises to the GOOD ear in sensorineural loss), and screen central red flags (focal neurology, severe vertigo/ataxia, sudden severe headache) that raise concern for a posterior-circulation stroke or cerebellopontine lesion needing emergency assessment. The examinable hidden agenda is minimisation ("just wax, not worried") masking a buried fear of "something in the brain" (a father’s stroke); screen the central features, address the fear, convey urgency without alarmism, and safety-net stroke red flags. SSNHL is treated with urgent (high-dose) corticosteroids, started by the specialist after audiometry, and benefits from EARLY treatment — ideally within days (ENT UK 2018: benefit is greatest when started early and is limited beyond about 2 weeks). Misattributing it to wax and booking routine syringing wastes the treatment window and can mean permanent deafness in that ear.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG98 Hearing loss in adults (2018) · ENT UK sudden sensorineural hearing loss guideline (2018) · NICE NG155 Tinnitus (2020)
knowledge.summary: Hearing loss in one ear that came on over 3 days or less is sudden sensorineural hearing loss until proven otherwise. It needs to be seen by ENT or the emergency department within 24 hours, not wax treatment.

points.t: NICE NG98: hearing loss that developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days → refer immediately, to be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department. Sudden loss more than 30 days ago, or loss worsening over 4 to 90 days → urgent referral, seen within 2 weeks. Damien’s loss is 2 days old: the 24-hour route applies.

ENT UK (2018): oral corticosteroid is the usual first treatment, started by the specialist after audiometry. Their suggested regimen is prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) for 7 days, then tapered over 5 days; intratympanic steroid is an option or salvage. Benefit is greatest when started early and is limited beyond about 2 weeks.

Wax usually builds gradually, often with a past history, and rarely causes tinnitus with unsteadiness. On the phone, ask him to hum: in sensorineural loss the sound is heard louder in the good ear; in conductive loss (wax, fluid) it is louder in the blocked ear. In clinic, Weber lateralises to the good ear and Rinne stays positive in sensorineural loss.

Sudden one-sided hearing loss with vertigo can rarely be a posterior-circulation stroke. Ask about facial or limb weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, trouble walking, and sudden severe headache. Any of these → 999 or the emergency department now, not an ENT slot.

Audiometry confirms the loss. NICE NG98: MRI of the internal auditory meatus is considered for asymmetric sensorineural loss (15 dB or more at 2 adjacent frequencies) to look for vestibular schwannoma; the specialist arranges this. NICE NG155 covers ongoing tinnitus support.
No syringing, irrigation, olive oil or cotton buds while this is assessed. They lose time and add nothing if the ear canal is clear.

dg.d: Open question about how the blocked feeling began before accepting “it’s wax”; lets him describe the sudden onset in his own words.
Teaching role and the pressure of term; effect of the hearing loss in class; what time off would mean to him.
Telephone hum test (Weber equivalent); plans audiometry via ENT; knows MRI of the internal auditory meatus follows for asymmetric loss (NICE NG98).
Wax or middle-ear fluid versus sensorineural loss versus a central cause; asks about wax history, discharge, a cold, pain.
Asks directly about focal weakness, numbness, speech, double vision, gait, severe vertigo and sudden headache (posterior-circulation stroke).
Names sudden sensorineural hearing loss and explains why it is not wax.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98); steroid treatment explained as time-critical; no syringing or drops.
Addresses the stroke fear with evidence; advises not driving while unsteady; offers a fit note for school.
Calls back with the appointment; emergency department fallback; named 999 stroke symptoms; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up the unsteadiness and the quick call despite “not worried”, which leads to his father’s stroke.
Idea (wax); the hidden fear of “something in the brain” linked to his father’s stroke; expectation of syringing or drops.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Mainly the hassle in a busy term. Underneath (only if asked): "Dad had a stroke — I did wonder if it was something in my head." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Damien Ofori? It’s Dr Shah from the surgery. Before we start, can I check your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk for ten minutes or so?
model.why: Telephone identity check and confirms a safe place to talk

model.text: Yes, I’m at home, it’s fine. My right ear’s gone all blocked and muffled, came on over a day or so, and there’s a ringing. I reckon it’s wax. Can you book me for syringing or tell me which drops to get?
Thanks, that’s a clear start. Can you tell me more about how it began, from the moment you first noticed it?
model.why: Open question before accepting the patient’s label

model.text: Two days ago. I was in class and it just went muffled over a few hours. The kids on that side sound miles away now. There’s a ringing and it feels full. No pain though.
Have you ever had wax trouble before, or a cold, any discharge, or put anything in the ear?
model.why: Tests the wax and conductive-cause hypothesis

model.text: No, never had wax problems. No cold, no discharge, nothing.
Can I try a quick test over the phone? Put the phone down for a second, and hum a low note with your mouth closed. Do you hear the hum louder in the right ear, the left ear, or the same in both?
model.why: Uses a telephone version of the Weber test to separate conductive from sensorineural loss

model.text: Hmm… it’s louder in the left. The good one.
That’s really helpful. You mentioned feeling a bit unsteady when you booked. Is the room spinning, or more a general wobbliness?
model.why: Characterises the dizziness to judge a central cause

model.text: Just a bit wobbly. Not spinning. I can walk fine.
Any weakness or numbness in your face, arms or legs? Slurred speech, double vision, trouble swallowing, or a sudden bad headache?
model.why: Screens central and stroke red flags explicitly

model.text: No, none of that.
I noticed you said you’re not too worried, but you rang quickly and you mentioned the unsteadiness. What has been going through your mind about it?
model.why: Picks up the gap between the minimising words and the behaviour

model.text: Honestly? My dad had a stroke. When it came on so suddenly and I felt wobbly, it did cross my mind it was something in the brain. I’d rather it was wax.

Thank you for telling me. That’s a very natural fear with your dad’s history, and I’m glad you said it out loud. The questions I just asked are the stroke warning signs, and you don’t have any of them today, which is reassuring.
model.why: Validates the hidden fear and links it to the evidence just gathered

model.text: Right. That does help.

Here’s what I think. The hum being louder in your good ear, the sudden start, the ringing and fullness with no wax history, all point away from wax. It sounds like the hearing nerve itself has been affected. That’s called sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
model.why: States the working diagnosis and the reasoning behind it

model.text: The nerve? So syringing won’t help?

No, and it could waste time. This is treated as urgent because the ear specialists can give a course of steroid tablets, and they work best the sooner they start. National guidance says you should be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department.
model.why: Applies the NICE NG98 24-hour rule and explains the treatment window

model.text: Within 24 hours? I’ve got teaching tomorrow.

I understand, and I know term is busy. But this is about keeping the hearing in that ear. A day or two can make a difference, and missing one day of school is much easier to put right than losing hearing. Could you manage to go today?
model.why: Conveys urgency without alarm and negotiates the barrier

model.text: Put like that, yes. I’ll sort cover.

Good. I’ll ring the on-call ENT team now and send them a letter with what we’ve discussed. I’ll call you back within the hour to tell you where and when. If I can’t reach them, you should go to the emergency department today.
model.why: Makes the referral concrete and has a fallback

model.text: Okay. Should I put drops in meanwhile?

No drops, no olive oil, nothing in the ear. They’ll do a proper hearing test, and if it confirms nerve hearing loss they’ll discuss steroids and a scan later on to check the nerve pathway. If you need a note for school, I can do that.
model.why: Stops harmful self-treatment and sets expectations for the next steps

model.text: One important thing. If before you’re seen you get weakness or numbness, a drooping face, slurred speech, double vision, severe spinning or you can’t walk straight, or a sudden severe headache, ring 999 straight away. Please don’t drive while you feel unsteady.
model.why: Specific 999 stroke safety-net in plain language, plus driving advice

model.text: Got it.
Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
It’s not wax, it might be the nerve, I’m being seen today by ENT, you’re ringing me back, nothing in the ear, and 999 if I get stroke signs.
Perfect. You rang expecting syringing; what we’re doing instead gives that ear the best chance. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Links the plan to his original request and offers the floor

model.text: No, that’s everything. Thanks for taking it seriously.

social.t: Teaching with one-sided hearing loss is tiring and can affect classroom control. Time off for urgent assessment is justified; a fit note can be issued if he cannot work.
His father’s stroke shapes how he reads the unsteadiness; the minimising is a way of coping with that fear.

legal.t: Advise him not to drive while unsteady. DVLA (Assessing fitness to drive): sudden disabling dizziness or vertigo that is likely to recur must be notified; mild unsteadiness that settles does not.

If hearing does not recover, permanent hearing loss that has a substantial long-term effect can count as a disability. His employer should then consider reasonable adjustments, and Access to Work can help with equipment.

professional.t: On the phone you cannot examine the ear, so reason from the history and a hum test, and act on the risk. Document the red-flag questions and his answers.
Make the referral yourself, give a fallback, and confirm he knows where to go. GMC Good medical practice: follow up on the actions you start.

community.t: RNID for information about sudden hearing loss and tinnitus; Tinnitus UK (formerly the British Tinnitus Association) for ongoing tinnitus support.

redFlags: Sudden onset over 3 days or less within the past 30 days: seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98)
Focal weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, ataxia, severe vertigo or sudden severe headache: possible posterior-circulation stroke, 999
Hum test louder in the good ear: points to sensorineural rather than conductive loss
psychosocial: Teacher mid-term who wants to avoid a fuss
Minimising (“just wax, not worried”) while clearly unsettled
Impact on work and daily life of hearing in one ear
ice: Concern: father’s stroke; fear it is “something in the brain”

playbook.diagnosis: “The sudden start, the ringing and fullness, no wax history, and the hum sounding louder in your good ear all point to the hearing nerve being affected, which we call sudden sensorineural hearing loss. It needs specialist assessment today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the ear as a microphone and a cable. Wax is like a cover over the microphone. This sounds more like the cable itself has had a sudden problem, and that needs the specialists quickly because the treatment works best early.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping this was simple wax, and with your dad’s stroke I completely understand why the suddenness frightened you. You don’t have any stroke warning signs today, and getting you checked properly is the best way to settle that worry.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the school pressure and help him make it work: a day off, a fit note if needed, and a clear explanation that the hearing in that ear may depend on acting now.
sharedPlan: Same-day ENT or emergency department assessment, within 24 hours (NICE NG98); GP phones ENT and calls him back
Audiometry, then specialist-led steroid treatment if confirmed (ENT UK 2018); MRI of the internal auditory meatus later for asymmetric loss
Nothing in the ear meanwhile; no driving while unsteady
safetyNet: 999 for facial droop, limb weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, severe vertigo or sudden severe headache
Go to the emergency department today if the ENT appointment cannot be arranged

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s label. “Wax” plus “no pain” pulls candidates into a routine plan, and the treatment window is lost. The patterns below come from recurring SCA feedback themes.

items.fail: Books syringing or recommends olive oil drops for two weeks on the patient’s say-so.
items.why: “Accepts the patient’s diagnosis without testing it.” Sudden one-sided loss over 3 days or less needs to be seen within 24 hours (NICE NG98).
items.fix: Ask about speed of onset and wax history, do the hum test, and say plainly: “I don’t think this is wax.”

items.fail: Refers to routine audiology or ENT “non-urgently”.
items.why: The steroid benefit falls away with time (ENT UK 2018). A routine wait is effectively no treatment.
items.fix: Name the time frame: “seen within 24 hours”. Phone ENT, and give the emergency department as the fallback.

items.fail: Never asks about stroke symptoms despite the unsteadiness.
items.why: “Did not rule out serious pathology.” Sudden hearing loss with vertigo can rarely be a posterior-circulation stroke.
items.fix: Ask each red flag directly: weakness, numbness, speech, double vision, walking, severe spinning, sudden headache.

items.fail: Takes “I’m not too worried” at face value.
items.why: “Does not identify or explore cues.” The hidden fear about his father’s stroke is the emotional centre of this case.
items.fix: Reflect the mismatch: “You say you’re not worried, but you rang quickly. What’s been going through your mind?”

items.fail: Insists on same-day attendance without hearing the school pressure, so he agrees on the phone and doesn’t go.
items.why: A plan he doesn’t own is a plan that fails. “Did not negotiate the management plan.”
items.fix: Acknowledge the barrier, explain what is at stake in one sentence, and help solve it (cover, fit note).

items.fail: Ends with “ring back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting is a standard failing statement, especially on the telephone.
items.fix: Specific 999 symptoms, an emergency department fallback, a promised call-back time, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: Identity check for the phone. Let him tell the story; “came on over a day”, the ringing and fullness are the key words.
Wax history, discharge, a cold, pain. Hum test on the phone. Character of the unsteadiness. Stroke red flags asked one by one.
Name the gap: “not worried” but he rang fast. Let the father’s stroke surface and answer it with the negative red flags.
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss, not wax. NICE NG98: seen within 24 hours. Negotiate the school barrier. Ring ENT; emergency department fallback.
Nothing in the ear. 999 stroke symptoms in plain words. No driving while unsteady. Call back with the appointment. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “wax” and books syringing or suggests olive oil drops; never asks when it started or whether it was sudden; no stroke red flags; misses the father’s stroke entirely; routine audiology referral or “see how it goes for two weeks”.
wordPics.pass: Recognises sudden one-sided hearing loss as an emergency, arranges ENT or emergency department assessment within 24 hours, asks about stroke symptoms, advises against syringing and gives a 999 safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus a telephone hum test to reason it through, surfaces the hidden stroke fear and answers it with the negative red flags, explains the steroid window in plain words, solves the school barrier, calls ENT personally with a fallback, and confirms the plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably wax. Use olive oil for two weeks and we’ll book syringing if it doesn’t clear.”
avoid.instead: “This came on suddenly without any wax history, so I want the ear specialists to see you today rather than treating it as wax.”
avoid.why: Two weeks of drops uses up the window when steroid treatment works best.

avoid.dont: “No pain, so nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “The lack of pain actually fits with the nerve being affected, which is why I’m taking it seriously.”
avoid.why: Sudden sensorineural loss is usually painless; pain is not the marker of urgency here.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, it’s definitely not a stroke.”
avoid.instead: “You don’t have any of the stroke warning signs today, which is reassuring; if any appear, ring 999.”
avoid.why: Honest, evidence-based reassurance with a safety-net beats a blanket promise you can’t make on the phone.

SCA_MODELS.text: Honestly? My dad had a stroke. When it came on so suddenly and I felt wobbly, it did cross my mind it was something in the brain. I’d rather it was wax.

Thank you for telling me. That’s a very natural fear with your dad’s history, and I’m glad you said it out loud. The questions I just asked are the stroke warning signs, and you don’t have any of them today, which is reassuring.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the hidden fear and links it to the evidence just gathered

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That does help.

Here’s what I think. The hum being louder in your good ear, the sudden start, the ringing and fullness with no wax history, all point away from wax. It sounds like the hearing nerve itself has been affected. That’s called sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
SCA_MODELS.why: States the working diagnosis and the reasoning behind it

SCA_MODELS.text: The nerve? So syringing won’t help?

No, and it could waste time. This is treated as urgent because the ear specialists can give a course of steroid tablets, and they work best the sooner they start. National guidance says you should be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department.
SCA_MODELS.why: Applies the NICE NG98 24-hour rule and explains the treatment window

SCA_MODELS.text: Within 24 hours? I’ve got teaching tomorrow.

I understand, and I know term is busy. But this is about keeping the hearing in that ear. A day or two can make a difference, and missing one day of school is much easier to put right than losing hearing. Could you manage to go today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Conveys urgency without alarm and negotiates the barrier

SCA_MODELS.text: Put like that, yes. I’ll sort cover.

Good. I’ll ring the on-call ENT team now and send them a letter with what we’ve discussed. I’ll call you back within the hour to tell you where and when. If I can’t reach them, you should go to the emergency department today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Makes the referral concrete and has a fallback

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Should I put drops in meanwhile?

No drops, no olive oil, nothing in the ear. They’ll do a proper hearing test, and if it confirms nerve hearing loss they’ll discuss steroids and a scan later on to check the nerve pathway. If you need a note for school, I can do that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Stops harmful self-treatment and sets expectations for the next steps

SCA_MODELS.text: One important thing. If before you’re seen you get weakness or numbness, a drooping face, slurred speech, double vision, severe spinning or you can’t walk straight, or a sudden severe headache, ring 999 straight away. Please don’t drive while you feel unsteady.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific 999 stroke safety-net in plain language, plus driving advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
It’s not wax, it might be the nerve, I’m being seen today by ENT, you’re ringing me back, nothing in the ear, and 999 if I get stroke signs.
Perfect. You rang expecting syringing; what we’re doing instead gives that ear the best chance. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Links the plan to his original request and offers the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s everything. Thanks for taking it seriously.

SCA_STEM.name: Damien Ofori
SCA_STEM.recent: Telephone triage request this morning: “right ear blocked for two days, thinks it is wax, wants syringing or drops”. No previous ear problems on the record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone consultation about a blocked right ear.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG98 Hearing loss in adults (2018) · ENT UK sudden sensorineural hearing loss guideline (2018) · NICE NG155 Tinnitus (2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Hearing loss in one ear that came on over 3 days or less is sudden sensorineural hearing loss until proven otherwise. It needs to be seen by ENT or the emergency department within 24 hours, not wax treatment.

points.t: NICE NG98: hearing loss that developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days → refer immediately, to be seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department. Sudden loss more than 30 days ago, or loss worsening over 4 to 90 days → urgent referral, seen within 2 weeks. Damien’s loss is 2 days old: the 24-hour route applies.

ENT UK (2018): oral corticosteroid is the usual first treatment, started by the specialist after audiometry. Their suggested regimen is prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) for 7 days, then tapered over 5 days; intratympanic steroid is an option or salvage. Benefit is greatest when started early and is limited beyond about 2 weeks.

Wax usually builds gradually, often with a past history, and rarely causes tinnitus with unsteadiness. On the phone, ask him to hum: in sensorineural loss the sound is heard louder in the good ear; in conductive loss (wax, fluid) it is louder in the blocked ear. In clinic, Weber lateralises to the good ear and Rinne stays positive in sensorineural loss.

Sudden one-sided hearing loss with vertigo can rarely be a posterior-circulation stroke. Ask about facial or limb weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, trouble walking, and sudden severe headache. Any of these → 999 or the emergency department now, not an ENT slot.

Audiometry confirms the loss. NICE NG98: MRI of the internal auditory meatus is considered for asymmetric sensorineural loss (15 dB or more at 2 adjacent frequencies) to look for vestibular schwannoma; the specialist arranges this. NICE NG155 covers ongoing tinnitus support.
No syringing, irrigation, olive oil or cotton buds while this is assessed. They lose time and add nothing if the ear canal is clear.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about how the blocked feeling began before accepting “it’s wax”; lets him describe the sudden onset in his own words.
Teaching role and the pressure of term; effect of the hearing loss in class; what time off would mean to him.
Picks up the unsteadiness and the quick call despite “not worried”, which leads to his father’s stroke.
Idea (wax); the hidden fear of “something in the brain” linked to his father’s stroke; expectation of syringing or drops.
Telephone hum test (Weber equivalent); plans audiometry via ENT; knows MRI of the internal auditory meatus follows for asymmetric loss (NICE NG98).
Wax or middle-ear fluid versus sensorineural loss versus a central cause; asks about wax history, discharge, a cold, pain.
Asks directly about focal weakness, numbness, speech, double vision, gait, severe vertigo and sudden headache (posterior-circulation stroke).
Names sudden sensorineural hearing loss and explains why it is not wax.
Seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98); steroid treatment explained as time-critical; no syringing or drops.
Addresses the stroke fear with evidence; advises not driving while unsteady; offers a fit note for school.
Calls back with the appointment; emergency department fallback; named 999 stroke symptoms; teach-back.

social.t: Teaching with one-sided hearing loss is tiring and can affect classroom control. Time off for urgent assessment is justified; a fit note can be issued if he cannot work.
His father’s stroke shapes how he reads the unsteadiness; the minimising is a way of coping with that fear.

legal.t: Advise him not to drive while unsteady. DVLA (Assessing fitness to drive): sudden disabling dizziness or vertigo that is likely to recur must be notified; mild unsteadiness that settles does not.

If hearing does not recover, permanent hearing loss that has a substantial long-term effect can count as a disability. His employer should then consider reasonable adjustments, and Access to Work can help with equipment.

professional.t: On the phone you cannot examine the ear, so reason from the history and a hum test, and act on the risk. Document the red-flag questions and his answers.
Make the referral yourself, give a fallback, and confirm he knows where to go. GMC Good medical practice: follow up on the actions you start.

community.t: RNID for information about sudden hearing loss and tinnitus; Tinnitus UK (formerly the British Tinnitus Association) for ongoing tinnitus support.

redFlags: Sudden onset over 3 days or less within the past 30 days: seen within 24 hours by ENT or the emergency department (NICE NG98)
Focal weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, ataxia, severe vertigo or sudden severe headache: possible posterior-circulation stroke, 999
Hum test louder in the good ear: points to sensorineural rather than conductive loss
psychosocial: Teacher mid-term who wants to avoid a fuss
Minimising (“just wax, not worried”) while clearly unsettled
Impact on work and daily life of hearing in one ear
ice: Concern: father’s stroke; fear it is “something in the brain”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The sudden start, the ringing and fullness, no wax history, and the hum sounding louder in your good ear all point to the hearing nerve being affected, which we call sudden sensorineural hearing loss. It needs specialist assessment today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the ear as a microphone and a cable. Wax is like a cover over the microphone. This sounds more like the cable itself has had a sudden problem, and that needs the specialists quickly because the treatment works best early.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping this was simple wax, and with your dad’s stroke I completely understand why the suddenness frightened you. You don’t have any stroke warning signs today, and getting you checked properly is the best way to settle that worry.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the school pressure and help him make it work: a day off, a fit note if needed, and a clear explanation that the hearing in that ear may depend on acting now.
sharedPlan: Same-day ENT or emergency department assessment, within 24 hours (NICE NG98); GP phones ENT and calls him back
Audiometry, then specialist-led steroid treatment if confirmed (ENT UK 2018); MRI of the internal auditory meatus later for asymmetric loss
Nothing in the ear meanwhile; no driving while unsteady
safetyNet: 999 for facial droop, limb weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, severe vertigo or sudden severe headache
Go to the emergency department today if the ENT appointment cannot be arranged

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s label. “Wax” plus “no pain” pulls candidates into a routine plan, and the treatment window is lost. The patterns below come from recurring SCA feedback themes.

items.fail: Books syringing or recommends olive oil drops for two weeks on the patient’s say-so.
items.why: “Accepts the patient’s diagnosis without testing it.” Sudden one-sided loss over 3 days or less needs to be seen within 24 hours (NICE NG98).
items.fix: Ask about speed of onset and wax history, do the hum test, and say plainly: “I don’t think this is wax.”

items.fail: Refers to routine audiology or ENT “non-urgently”.
items.why: The steroid benefit falls away with time (ENT UK 2018). A routine wait is effectively no treatment.
items.fix: Name the time frame: “seen within 24 hours”. Phone ENT, and give the emergency department as the fallback.

items.fail: Never asks about stroke symptoms despite the unsteadiness.
items.why: “Did not rule out serious pathology.” Sudden hearing loss with vertigo can rarely be a posterior-circulation stroke.
items.fix: Ask each red flag directly: weakness, numbness, speech, double vision, walking, severe spinning, sudden headache.

items.fail: Takes “I’m not too worried” at face value.
items.why: “Does not identify or explore cues.” The hidden fear about his father’s stroke is the emotional centre of this case.
items.fix: Reflect the mismatch: “You say you’re not worried, but you rang quickly. What’s been going through your mind?”

items.fail: Insists on same-day attendance without hearing the school pressure, so he agrees on the phone and doesn’t go.
items.why: A plan he doesn’t own is a plan that fails. “Did not negotiate the management plan.”
items.fix: Acknowledge the barrier, explain what is at stake in one sentence, and help solve it (cover, fit note).

items.fail: Ends with “ring back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting is a standard failing statement, especially on the telephone.
items.fix: Specific 999 symptoms, an emergency department fallback, a promised call-back time, and teach-back.
